sentences.text: Mekosuchus is an extinct genus of crocodiles that lived in Australasia.
These animals were generally small, terrestrial creatures under two meters long, featuring short, blunt snouts and powerful limbs.
Unlike the elongated, flattened skulls of most modern crocodiles, Mekosuchus possessed a short, raised skull shape.
The nostrils and eyes were positioned on the front and sides of the skull, indicating it was not built for an aquatic lifestyle.
The oldest species had blade-like teeth with flattened sides designed for slicing.
Despite its small size, Mekosuchus likely possessed very strong neck muscles based on its vertebrae structure.
M. inexpectatus possessed specialized back teeth adapted for cracking hard-shelled invertebrates like molluscs, crustaceans, and insects, unlike the bladed teeth of mainland species.
Due to its small size, Mekosuchus likely used headshaking rather than the death roll maneuver to feed, as the latter is less effective in animals smaller than three to four meters.
The neck of M. whitehunterensis suggests it was adapted to tearing flesh from carcasses by violently shaking its head while sharp teeth cut the food.
The first fossil bone of Mekosuchus, a fragmentary quadratojugal, was collected from Kanumera Bay in New Caledonia in 1981.
In 2007, researchers reconstructed the skull of M. inexpectatus as resembling modern dwarf crocodiles after finding new fossil remains.
Radiocarbon dating suggests M. inexpectatus fossils from the Isle of Pines date to roughly 3,750 years before present.
In 1995, Paul Willis hypothesized that Mekosuchus might have been arboreal and filled a niche similar to modern monitor lizards.
Holt and colleagues suggest that Mekosuchus inexpectatus may have lived a lifestyle similar to modern dwarf crocodiles or dwarf caimans.
Holt and colleagues hypothesize that Mekosuchus inexpectatus inhabited slow-moving streams in New Caledonia rainforests and foraged at night near water and on land.
Mekosuchus whitehunterensis is believed to have possessed strong neck muscles used for ripping flesh from carcasses.
Mekosuchus resembled dwarf caimans and crocodiles in size and ecology, making them potentially easier prey for humans than larger continental crocodilians.

Although it is not certain if mekosuchines possessed adaptations or tolerance for saltwater like modern crocodiles, it remains possible they swam directly between islands or arrived via natural rafts.
Both processes could have taken advantage of low sea levels in the late Cenozoic, reducing the distance between islands and at times joining island chains into one.
Researchers initially classified Mekosuchus as an early eusuchian and placed it in its own family, Mekosuchidae, due to its unique anatomy.
The genus Mekosuchus was established by Balouet and Buffetaut in 1987.
Due to poor preservation and overlapping ranges, some researchers suggest M. kalpokasi may be synonymous with M. inexpectatus.
Mekosuchus fossils range from the Oligocene to the Holocene, with survival until approximately 1,700 years ago being possible but unconfirmed.
Mekosuchus likely went extinct around 3,000 years ago during the Holocene, though some authors suggest they may have survived more recently.
Fossil evidence indicates that Mekosuchus originated on mainland Australia, but its dispersal throughout the South Pacific is poorly understood.
The cause of Mekosuchus extinction is debated; while some suggest human involvement, others note insufficient evidence of overlap with human settlements and lack of direct signs of human impact.
There is significant disagreement among researchers regarding the exact shape of the Mekosuchus skull, with published reconstructions differing greatly.
It is debated whether mekosuchines actively swam between landmasses or drifted using natural rafts to disperse.
